conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having trouble swallowing and some pain when you eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's been going on for weeks. Food feels stuck in my throat, especially solids. And it hurts right at my trach site when I swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned liquids sometimes go down the wrong way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, not like choking, but I feel them going into my airway. It’s scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of tracheobronchomalacia and tracheostomy, we need to be careful. We’ve ordered a chest X-ray to check for infection or other issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Could this be related to my trach or past surgeries?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Scar tissue or inflammation from prior reconstructions could affect swallowing. We’ll look into that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray came back. Good news — no pneumonia or lung issues. Your trach and Port-A-Cath are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why am I still having trouble swallowing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it might be related to swelling or reflux. You’ve had GERD before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I’ve been feeling more heartburn lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. We’re going to start you on a higher dose of your reflux medication for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the pain when I swallow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should, over a few days. But we also want to do a swallowing study with barium to see exactly what’s happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my trach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very safe. A speech therapist will help guide it. We need to check if food or liquid is going into your airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. We’ve scheduled your swallowing study for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve been sticking to soft foods and thickened liquids. It helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s smart. We’ll keep you on that until we get more answers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your swallowing study was done this morning. I have the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? Did you see where the problem is?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The upper part of your throat is quite swollen, which explains the feeling of food getting stuck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. There’s no sign of infection. But we did see that stomach contents are coming all the way up into your throat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s why things taste sour sometimes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And that acid is probably causing the swelling and pain. We also saw a small hiatal hernia, which can make reflux worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a fistula? I was worried food might be going into my trach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad you asked. The study shows no tracheoesophageal fistula. That’s a relief. But we did see thin liquids penetrating into your airway, though not full aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means we need to keep using thickened liquids and soft foods for now. The speech therapist will give you specific instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the reflux? Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re already treating it with stronger medication. Over time, that should reduce the swelling and improve swallowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery for the hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll manage it medically first. If symptoms persist, your gastroenterologist can discuss options later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your dentist noted a possible abscess on one of your teeth. Have you had tooth pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Now that you mention it, yes — my lower right molar has been aching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be contributing to the discomfort when you swallow. We’ll note it for your dentist to treat after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you this evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the reflux medication, stick to soft foods and thickened liquids, and follow up with your pulmonologist and primary care provider.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tooth?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your dentist soon for the abscess. We’ll send them a note.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure you have all the instructions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you’re cleared to go home. Nurse will give you discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll follow everything you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Call us if swallowing gets worse or you develop fever or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.
